en: Commentary on the *Śataśāstra*, Scroll One.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Wenguī of Ximing Monastery.
Chapter One: Refuting Permanence. Originally composed by Āryadeva Bodhisattva; explained by Dharmapāla Bodhisattva.
As for what Shu said:
the original treatise by Āryadeva consists of two hundred verses;
twenty-five verses are composed as a single chapter.
There are eight chapters in total,
which are broadly divided into two parts.
The first seven chapters extensively refute the doctrines of the heterodox schools.
The final chapter extensively establishes the correct principles;
among these, it refutes heterodox schools.
Of the preceding two chapters, the first two refute the doctrine of permanence.
Of the five subsequent chapters that refute the impermanent,
within the refutation of the permanent,
the first chapter generally refutes all forms of permanence.
The final chapter separately refutes the self and permanence;
this present "Refutation of Permanence" chapter is precisely that which previously refuted all forms of permanence in general.
Dharmapāla’s commentary on the treatise consists of more than three thousand stanzas.
The explanation of the main text is divided into three parts.
First, the two lines of verse paying homage to Āryadeva constitute the introduction.
Second, the commentary states: "In order to manifest... and so forth.
The explanation of the root verses constitutes the main body (the *śarīra*).
The subsequent section beginning with "Those who possess the great resolve" and below,
which exhorts study and the making of vows, constitutes the dissemination (the *pariṇāmana*).
The treatise says:
"I bow my head to the One of Sublime Wisdom... I shall now provide an exposition. The commentary states:
This expression of homage to the Holy Deva constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, being about to explain the treatise composed by the Bodhisattva Āryadeva,
first offers a verse of homage to express his utmost sincerity.
The first three lines constitute this expression of reverence.
The following phrase explains "reverence.
As for "sublime wisdom" (*prajñā*):
because the Bodhisattva Āryadeva has penetrated both the ultimate truth and conventional reality, he is said to possess "sublime wisdom."
This is a direct eulogy.
The phrase "like the solar orb casting light to shatter darkness and open the pure eye" is a metaphorical illustration.
Just as the solar orb in the world has two functions:
first, it radiates light to dispel darkness;
second, it illuminates forms to open the eyes.
"The one who widely disseminated subtle words and extensively expounded the *Śataśāstra* [is Āryadeva];
this is a collective description.
The sublime wisdom of Āryadeva is likewise."
First, by disseminating subtle words, he shatters the darkness of ignorance;
second, by illuminating the ultimate and conventional truths, he opens the eye of wisdom.
As for "the words spreading afar":
The treatise composed by Deva was transmitted eight hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa and reached a period of one thousand years; hence it is said to have spread far and wide.
As for "subtle words," this treatise not only refutes existence but also dispels non-existence.
Because all attachments are eliminated and every word spoken is appropriate, they are called "subtle words" (*sūkṣma-vākya*).
As for the *Śata-śāstra*,
Deva composed a total of one hundred treatises, all of which are titled *Śata-śāstra*.
Furthermore, a hundred sages have followed and practiced this path without ever deviating from it;
thus, it is called the *Śata-śāstra*.
This is intended to manifest its manifold nature, rather than to imply that the number of sections is exactly one hundred.
It is like the fact that the hundred kings do not change [their laws] and the hundred flavors of food remain constant;
yet, distinct titles have been prefixed to these various versions of the *Śata-śāstra*,
such as the old *Śata-śāstra* being called the *Sūtra-śata-śāstra*.
Because that which is spoken in prose directly is called *sūtra*, that treatise states: *sūtra*.
*Sūtra* is precisely the same as "scripture" (*jing*).
The old [translation] states:
"Because this treatise contains one hundred verses, it is named 'The Hundred' (*Śataśāstra*).
This treatise consists of twenty chapters, each containing five verses."
The claim that "the final ten chapters are not translated because they are useless" is an error.
Upon examining the Sanskrit original, there are only ten chapters;
furthermore, this treatise consists of eight chapters.
This treatise consists of twenty-five chapters and a total of two hundred verses.
How can it be said that the name "Hundred" is derived from the fact that the treatise contains one hundred stanzas?
Furthermore, the old *Śatapañcāśatikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (The Perfection of Wisdom in One Hundred and Fifty Verses) should likewise be named the *Śata Sūtra*.
When Deva was approaching his death, he wrote his name in blood.
Since this treatise consists of exactly one hundred characters and follows the practice of the hundred sages, it is called the *Śataśāstra* (Treatise of One Hundred Characters).

Furthermore, for the sake of a king’s crown prince who wept incessantly over his father’s funeral, he composed a treatise to instruct him; thus it was named the *Śata-śāstra* (Treatise in One Hundred Verses).
Now, this *Śata-śāstra* is both exhaustive in its elucidation of principles and extensive in its refutation of dogmatic attachments.
Thus it is called the *Śataka-śāstra* (The Treatise in One Hundred Verses).
Regarding the phrase "I shall explain [it] as the hundred sages have practiced," this expresses an act of reverence.
I shall now provide an exposition of the *Śataśāstra-vṛtti-vaipulya* (The Hundred-Verse Treatise on the Conduct of the Hundred Sages) composed by Deva;
therefore, I proffer this homage.
The treatise says:
The *Śāstra* says: "In order to manifest the attainment [of the goal], this treatise is composed. The *Vyākhyā* states:
From here below is the explanation of the root verses, which constitutes the main body of the work (*siddhānta*). It consists of three parts:
first, the narration of the intent for composing the treatise.
Second, to clarify the sequence of the chapters, the verses are cited for individual explanation.
Within the exposition of the intent of the treatise’s composition, there is first the statement of the thesis and subsequently its explanation.
This is the heading.

Both the dual attachments to persons and phenomena involve the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," which collectively encompass all objects of the pervasive conceptualization (parikalpita-svabhāva) without exception.
Because both the essential nature and the appearances of this thoroughly imagined nature are entirely non-existent, they are said to be "all empty.
Because this principle of emptiness reveals the three gates of liberation, it is said to be "skillfully revealed."
This is the intention behind Āryadeva’s composition of the treatise.
The treatise states:
"When one clings to the nature of things as real entities, both [subject and object] are non-existent. The commentary says:
This is the explanation.
Because one takes the two types of entities— person and phenomena— as the means,
there arises the conceptual discrimination of the ten signs, such as male and female, form, sound, and fragrance.
Because one relies on the ten aspects of conceptual differentiation regarding the substantial nature of the two types of grasping,
one gives rise to perverse aspirations, such as wishing to become a celestial king or a human king.
Once the emptiness of the substantial nature of both persons and phenomena has been revealed, the gate of liberation that is emptiness is thereby revealed.
The tenfold conceptual differentiation is simultaneously extinguished, thereby manifesting the gate of liberation of signlessness (animitta-vimokṣamukha).
Since all objective characteristics are thus seen as nothing to be sought or desired,
this manifests the gate of liberation of wishlessness (apraṇihita-vimokṣamukha).
Therefore it is said that since both phenomena (*dharma*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*) are revealed to be non-existent, the two attachments are [eliminated].
The meaning of the gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) is explained extensively elsewhere.
The treatise states:
Regarding the statement, "That which belongs to the self must first destroy the notion of permanence":
the commentary states that this demonstrates the sequence of the chapters.
Those who have generated attachment and delight are difficult to liberate.
Those who have given rise to revulsion and detachment find it easy to relinquish [their attachments].
Therefore, at the beginning of this treatise, we first refute the "permanence" that is difficult to eliminate regarding what is clung to as "self" and "what belongs to the self.
As stated previously, these are the entities of "self" and "mine."
Regarding the current statement "that which belongs to my self":
previously, this was based on the distinction between grasping at the view of a self and that which belongs to the self;
now, following the abbreviated text, "self" is omitted, and it simply says "that which belongs to my self."
Question:
Since it is said to be "brief," why does it not say "I" but rather "mine"?
Answer: The designation "mine" (mama) is broad, encompassing both the internal and the external;
the designation "self" (ātman) is narrow, not extending to the external.
Therefore, it does not say "I.
The *Śāstra* says:
"Thus, a verse is spoken, from '...to the true name, Tathāgata'... The commentary says:
The following section provides a detailed explanation through verses.
There are twenty-five verses in total;
the first five verses generally refute the notion of permanence.
The final twenty verses specifically refute permanence.
Within the general refutation, one verse is divided into five parts;
the first verse refutes [permanence] by means of its production of effects.
The second verse refutes [the argument] by means of existence;
the third verse refutes it by means of the absence of a cause;
the fourth verse refutes it by means of the lack of an example.
The fifth section, consisting of one verse, refutes [the opponent's position] by means of the distinction between the ignorant and the wise.
The argument that "arising as an effect" constitutes the primary refutation of intrinsic existence (*svabhāva*), while "existence itself" serves as a secondary refutation.
The point regarding "lack of cause" demonstrates that the heterodox school's tenet cannot be established.
The "Omission of the Simile" (kūpamāna) reveals that the reason [adduced by the opponent] is contradictory.
"Foolish and Wise" refutes and censures the externalist.
Regarding the refutation of the production of an effect, first the verse is presented, followed by its explanation.
This is the citation of the verse.
The first half establishes the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
the second half offers praise to a single person.
The two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) refer to inference (*anumāna*) and authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*).
The "one person" refers to the Tathāgata.
"All that arises for the sake of a result" [refers to all phenomena].
This establishes a formal inference (prayoga) to correctly refute the Vaiśeṣika and other schools' claim that produced effects are eternal phenomena.
They establish six categories (padārtha):
first, substance (dravya), which consists of nine entities.
These are earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, mind, and self.
The second category, the qualities (*guṇa*), comprises more than twenty factors, namely:

color, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, suffering, pleasure, greed, hatred, delusion, number, dimension, conjunction, disjunction, separateness, cognition, effort, slackness, dexterity, clumsiness, and so forth.
The three types of action (*karma*) refer to going and coming, slow and fast movement, bending and stretching, looking up and looking down, and so forth.
The four kinds of existence (*bhava*) refer to substance, quality, action, and intrinsic nature; because these are not non-existent, they are termed "existence."
Thus, there exists a nature that is neither real nor [identical to] qualities or activities,
which possesses a distinct substantial essence (*svabhāva*) pervading all phenomena. Fifth is "sameness and difference" (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*).
In terms of the real as it relates to the real, they are identical;
in terms of the real as it relates to qualities and so forth, they are different.
Such identity and difference are likewise not the prior real and so forth.
There exists a distinct intrinsic nature;
thus, it exists separately upon each individual phenomenon.
What was formerly called the "truth of general characteristics" and the "truth of specific characteristics" refers to this.
This refers precisely to the two propositions of "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) and "Identity/Difference" (tādātmya-tadutpatti).
The sixth, "conjunction" (saṃyoga), means that when a self and dharmas conjoin, the nature of conjunction arises;
it is like the nature of conjunction among the Saṃgha according to the Sarvāstivāda school.
The two categories of substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) are generally impermanent.
That is to say, within the category of substances, the five—space, time, direction, mind, and self—are invariably eternal;
whereas earth, water, fire, and wind, as the four great elements, are both eternal and impermanent.
This means that during the kalpa of emptiness, there are four atoms scattered here and there.
When the subsequent kalpa of formation begins, the karmic power of sentient beings causes these atoms to pair up and combine, each producing a single subtle fruit.
One of these minute fruits is equal in measure to two atoms (*paramāṇu*).
Such minute fruits further combine in pairs to produce coarser fruits;
thus increasing gradually, they eventually aggregate to produce the receptacle world (*bhājana-loka*).
At the time when the subsequent kalpa is destroyed, the most coarse and large fruits are first destroyed by the calamities;
gradually, the destruction reaches the initial subtle fruits until all fruits,
both coarse and subtle, are completely exhausted.
The most subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) are not subject to destruction by calamities;
thus, these atoms of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternal,
while the effects produced from them are all impermanent.
Within the category of quality (guṇa), it is said that the substance of number (saṃkhyā) pervades all substances, qualities, and actions;
furthermore, as with the subtle quality upon an atom, this [substance] is also eternal.
All other things, such as suffering and pleasure, form, sound, fragrance, and so forth, are impermanent.
Great Existence (Mahā-bhūta), along with its similarities and differences, is exclusively eternal.
Karma and their conjunction are exclusively impermanent.
What is being refuted here is merely its permanence.
Within this permanence, there is the permanence that produces effects and the permanence that does not produce effects;
for example, the atoms of the four great elements are able to produce subtle effects.
Space produces the quality of sound;
the self produces the quality of volition;
and time produces the quality of sprouting—these are called "producing fruits" and are eternal.

For example, such things as "existence" (sattā), "sameness" (sāmānya) and "difference" (viśeṣa), the qualities of minuteness (aṇutva) and pervasiveness (mahatva), as well as number (saṃkhyā) and so forth, merely manifest upon substances and the like;
they cannot produce others and are therefore called "non-productive" (akārya) and "eternal" (nitya).
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins and others establish that even things such as space (*ākāśa*), nirvāṇa, and pleasure are unarisen and eternal fruits.
When we say "all" here, it refers to those like arisen fruits, atoms, and so forth.
This is precisely the subject of the proposition (*dharmin*).
As for "arising," this arising of the resultant atom (*paramāṇu*) should arise from another.
This is the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).
This conjunction constitutes the formal proposition (*pratijñā*). "That which is produced as an effect" [is the reason].
This is because the effect of the atom arises from this [cause].
This intention also includes the word "arising" (*jāyamāna*) from the thesis (*pakṣa*) as an auxiliary factor for establishing the reason.
The verse is concise and does not mention the two examples.
Alternatively, it may be that the statement "all arise" constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*), while "because they arise from a single [cause]" constitutes the reason (*hetu*).
That is to say: because all these effects arise from this [single cause].
This intention takes both the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the produced effect of the example (*dṛṣṭānta-phala*) as assisting in the establishment of the reason (*hetu*).
The single character "effect" (*phala*) serves as the common feature of the example (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*);
that is to say, because an effect produced from two atoms (*paramāṇu*) onward is capable of producing something else.
This takes "arising from another" as the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). The verse omits the counter-illustration (*vipakṣa*) for brevity. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is:

"All permanent phenomena that produce effects arise from conditions. The reason (*hetu*) is: "Because they are capable of producing effects. The similar illustration (*sapakṣa*) is: "Just like coarse fruits, all things capable of producing effects arise from conditions. The counter-illustration (*vipakṣa*) is: "If they do not arise from conditions, they do not produce effects, such as flowers in the sky (*khapuṣpa*). By means of this inference (*anumāna*), it is established that permanent phenomena which produce effects must necessarily arise from conditions; having arisen, they return to extinction.
This definitively states that [all things] are impermanent.
As for the reason why they possess the nature of impermanence,
this cites authoritative scripture (*āptavacana*) to establish the aforementioned inference (*anumāna*).
According to the principles of inference, since all phenomena are impermanent,
the Buddha's wisdom is also impermanent;
thus it is spoken in accordance with reason.
Not only is the word of the Sage established by inference,
but inference is also established by the word of the Sage.
Therefore, apart from the Buddha, there is no one who can truly be called a Tathāgata.
This praises a single individual.
The Buddha has realized impermanence and teaches the principle of impermanence exactly as it is; for this reason alone he is called the Tathāgata.
Apart from the Buddha, the teachers of other paths speak in ways that deviate from the truth and are therefore not Tathāgatas.
Question:
Since the Buddha’s five eyes are perfectly clear and his six supernormal powers are fully perfected, such that he perceives all objects without obstruction and is uniquely titled the Tathāgata,
why does the verse not first praise him at the outset, but instead offers its eulogy only after the section on inference (*anumāna*)?
Answer: If one were addressing our own school, one would first praise the Buddha and then discuss the Dharma;
now, in addressing non-Buddhists, one establishes the principles first and then extols the person.
This is truly because principles cannot be discussed in isolation, while people have their own partialities;
therefore, one first establishes the underlying principles and only then praises the person.
As the treatise says:
The Treatise says: "All that exists is established through direct perception and inference. The Commentary says:
The following is the explanation; first, the verse is explained, and subsequently, objections are addressed.
The commentary on the verse consists of three parts:
first, the explanation of the first line;
second, the explanation of the second line.
Next, the two subsequent phrases are explained.
Regarding the first phrase, the initial section provides the direct explanation.
Next, the refutation follows;
finally, the intended meaning is revealed.
The formal explanation shows that the phenomenon which arises does so from arising itself.
The refutation by way of return (pratyāpatti-viparyaya) serves to show that non-arising phenomena do not exist;
the clarification of the intended meaning serves to show that arising phenomena return to cessation.
In the primary explanation, the initial presentation of the [wrong] views explains the two characters "all" (sarva).
Subsequently, he correctly refutes the literal interpretation of the three characters "fruit-arising" (*phala-utpāda*).
"Worldly" refers to the false and illusory;
"base attachment" refers to evil views.
"Other proponents" refers to the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) and those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).
"Permanent entities" refers to such things as atoms (*paramāṇu*).
This means that the falsely held and erroneous views of others—such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others—which differ from the Mahāyāna school, assert that atoms and so forth are permanent.
For the most part, these are not apprehended by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the five sense-faculties or the five consciousnesses.
For example, atoms, space, time, direction, mind, self, subtle spheres,
and qualities are none of them apprehended by the direct perception of the physical sense-faculties.
Regarding their similarities and differences: if [the object] is based on form and so forth that are visible and so forth, it is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
if it is based on atoms (*paramāṇu*) that are invisible and so forth, it is not apprehended by direct perception.
Therefore, it is said that [the object] largely transcends the domain of what is accessible to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Since atoms and the like are not apprehended by direct perception,
how can there be a cognition that perceives them?
This is established through inference based on the production of effects.
That is to say, it is observed in the world that coarse effects such as vases are never produced without depending upon their subtle causes, such as atoms.
Therefore, one knows that the third subtle effect likewise depends upon the first two extreme atoms for its production.
Furthermore, if there were no mind (*manas*) and no self (*ātman*),
from whom would suffering and pleasure, or good and evil, arise?
And if there were no space (*ākāśa*), from what would sound originate?
If time did not exist, how could sprouts and the like arise? To establish this through inference (*anumāna*), one states:

"The third [category], subtle effects such as suffering, pleasure, and sound, necessarily have a cause" is the thesis (*pakṣa*); "because they are effects" is the reason (*hetu*); "just like gross effects" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore: "Subtle particles (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth, their essence necessarily exists" is the thesis; "because they are capable of producing effects" is the reason; "just like gross effects" is the example.
The Treatise says:
"Since it can produce effects such as coarse form (*rūpa*) and so forth. The Commentary states:
This is the actual refutation.
That which is capable of producing a fruit is precisely what establishes the cause;
one should likewise infer that whatever arises from conditions must also be so produced.
This constitutes the thesis (*pakṣa*).
"Such as coarse form, etc. constitutes the similar example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*).
The treatise says:
"If it were not dependently arisen, it would be like a flower in the sky," and so forth. The commentary states:
This is a refutation by way of contraposition.
If you dogmatically maintain that the eternal entity which produces effects does not arise from conditions, then [the syllogism would be]:

"The eternal entity that produces effects lacks superior essence and function" (thesis), "because it does not arise from conditions" (reason), "like a flower in the sky" (example). Alternatively, one might use this refutation as a prior formal argument: "The eternal entity that produces effects cannot produce effects" (thesis), "because it does not arise from conditions" (reason), "because it lacks essence and function" (reason), "like a flower in the sky" (example). Thus, one may employ this text as a counter-argument.
The negative example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is formulated as previously explained in the verse.
The opponent originally sought to prove that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth definitely exist by using the reason (*hetu*) of their capacity to produce effects.

Here, "atoms and so forth" constitute the subject (*dharmin*), and "existence" constitutes the property (*dharma*) of that subject; within this subject-property complex, the statement "is" (*asti*) manifests that this is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property itself.
However, [the opponent] intends to admit that this "existence" does not arise from conditions; this is precisely a distinction among phenomena (*dharma-viśeṣa*).
Now, the Master of the Treatise (Vasubandhu) employs that very same reason to refute the claim that atoms and so forth arise from conditions.
This entails the fault of contradicting the distinct characteristics of external causes and their effects.
The treatise says:
"If one were to grant that [the cause] reaches [the state of] the produced effect as it is described. The commentary states:
This clarifies the intended meaning:
the verse establishes that one should desire for the mind to return immediately to cessation.
If you, being constrained by reason, concede that atoms and so forth arise from conditions, [then...]
This should be understood as following the natural principle that whatever gross fruit is produced must inevitably return to extinction.
The Treatise says:
"Therefore, the Buddha spoke of [everything] up to suffering, pleasure, and so forth. The Commentary states:
This explains the second line of the verse.
Since the principles of inference have been established,
it is clearly known that the words of the Sage are not erroneous.
Since the Buddha has already made this sincere declaration,
why do you harbor doubts?
The arising of suffering and pleasure is necessarily impermanent.
Because the Vaiśeṣika school is the same as the preceding [case], it is cited as an analogy.
The treatise says:
"Therefore, only the Buddha reaches the state of being unimpeded. The commentary states:
This explains the following two lines.
Only the Buddha alone possesses the two wisdoms of *yathābhūta* (as it is) and *yāvadbhāvikatā* (as far as it extends), which perceive the two realms of truth and conventionality without obstruction.
Because he speaks in accordance with what he perceives, he is named the Tathāgata.
The *Śāstra* says:
"If that is so, the remaining [factors] arise from conditions. The commentary states:
The following passage addresses an external objection.
First the objection, then the resolution.
This is the objection:
the outsider says.
If it is argued that because atoms and the like produce effects,
they are impermanent— just as coarse effects arise from conditions— then, according to our own school,
the remaining categories such as "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) and "Specific Universality" (sāmānyaviśeṣa), which do not produce effects, [would likewise be permanent].
This [Great Existence, etc. must be eternal;
for since Great Existence and the like do not produce effects, they cannot be inferred to arise from conditions by analogy with gross effects.
The intent of this objection is as follows:
while atoms (*paramāṇu*) may produce effects and thus be impermanent,
the Great Existent (*mahāsattā*) does not produce effects and therefore ought to be permanent.
This should be understood as a critique of the meaning of the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).
Furthermore, the Sarvāstivādins and others raise the following objection:
"While it may be granted that the atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the Vaiśeṣika school can produce effects and are therefore impermanent," [the opponent's position remains untenable].
"In our school, space and nirvāṇa do not produce effects; therefore, they must be permanent.
The treatise says:
"Even so, since there is no reaching [of them], they should be inferred to be non-existent. The commentary states:
This applies to your own school as well.
Although within your school there are such things as the "Great Existence" (mahāsattā) which does not produce effects,
according to the Sarvāstivādins and others, space and nirvana should likewise be eternal.
However, since certain things lack the functional capacity to produce an effect—
just like a rabbit’s horn— they must be inferred to be non-existent, as they possess neither past existence nor cessation.

The Mahābhūta-nature and such, as well as space and the like, are all non-existent, because the school [of the opponent] holds that there is no causal function for the production of an effect; thus, the reason is like that which has been eternally extinguished, and there is no corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
The treatise says:
"In order to clarify this statement, it is further stated in verse: [The commentary continues: "The explanation states:"
The following second verse refutes [the opponent's position] by means of its having an existent nature; that is,
it assists the preceding verse in refuting the permanence of that which produces an effect,
while also incidentally refuting the permanence of that which does not produce an effect.
First, the initial arising;
second, the citation of the verse;
and finally, the explanation.
This is the arising [of the effect].
Fearing that outsiders might still cling to the notion that there are both permanent effects produced and impermanent effects produced,
how can one use the impermanent as an analogy for the permanent?
Furthermore, there are fruits that always arise and fruits that never arise.
Although the permanence of arising fruits may be refuted,
these non-arising fruits cannot be refuted.
This verse is now stated again both to demonstrate the certainty of the preceding verse’s refutation of the claim that produced effects are permanent,
and also to simultaneously demonstrate the certainty of this refutation of the claim that unproduced effects are permanent.
The Treatise says:
"There is no time, place, or entity that reaches the state of having an intrinsic nature and remains eternally.
Commentary: This cites the verse.
The first half [of the verse] establishes that existing phenomena arise from conditions;
the second half establishes that what has arisen must inevitably return to cessation.
"Time" refers to the four seasons, such as spring and summer, and the three periods, such as the past.
"Directions" refers to the ten directions, such as east and west;
"things" refers to all entities such as the sense faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), form (*rūpa*), and mind (*citta*).

This statement means that there are no entities—whether belonging to the three times, the four seasons, or the ten directions, or consisting of faculties, objects, form, or mind—that exist inherently rather than being dependently originated.
Therefore, one should know that there is no time, place, or category of thing produced from conditions that does not ultimately return to extinction and remain eternally abiding.
The treatise says:
"All things that exist... should arise from conditions. The commentary states: [As follows].
The following is the commentary,
which consists of four parts.
The first is the explanation of the verses.
Second, the summary of the meaning of the verse; third, the demonstration of the verse’s completion;
fourth, the citation of the verse as proof.
Within the commentary on the verse text, there are two interpretations.
First, existence is used to prove dependent origination;
later, dependent origination is used to prove existence.

This means that what they have established—time, space, and categories of things—are all the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective images) manifested by the consciousness-mind, and thus their nature is that of being dependent on another (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that time, direction, substance, and so forth definitely arise from conditions; the reason (*hetu*) is "because they possess existence" (*sattvāt*); the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is that all things possessing existence arise from conditions, such as suffering and pleasure; and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is that if something does not arise from conditions, it lacks existence, such as a flower in the sky. In this context, one should formulate a general inference as follows:

"The whole [as a partless] space is established as having infinite parts, because it is inseparable from its infinite parts; the reason is like the various parts themselves. Furthermore, one should formulate separate inferences as follows:

The space conjoined with a single portion of springtime possesses parts; it necessarily lacks the property of being conjoined with a portion of autumn, because it is inseparable from the portion of springtime. This is like the case of the portion of springtime; other times, such as the season of autumn, can be understood by analogy.
The treatise says:
"Do not let this [principle] apply to all associated [factors]. The commentary states:
This is a refutation by means of analogy.
If you stubbornly maintain that a single part of emptiness is universally associated with all parts,
then you must likewise allow each of those associated parts to be universally associated with everything.

This means that each individual part should be established as possessing a whole (*sāvayava*), because the thesis [that it possesses a whole] is inseparable from the emptiness of the whole (*sāvayava-śūnyatā*); thus, the reason (*hetu*) is like the example of the emptiness of the whole, and one should further formulate this inference separately.

This means that a portion of spring should not be separated from the other three seasons, just as the thesis (pakṣa) is not separated from its constituent parts; because the reason (hetu) is like the empty space of a part, the analogy (dṛṣṭānta)—such as the remaining seasons, the directions, and so forth—should be formulated in this very way.
The *Śāstra* says:
"Therefore, this partitive division reaches the point of becoming immeasurable divisions. The commentary states:
This explains the second half of the verse, which serves as the conclusion of the refutation.
The initial statement is followed by an explanation;
this is the formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*).
Because it conforms to its various parts, it possesses these parts, which are thus divided into infinite portions.
The treatise says:
"These very parts, upon reaching completion, become other categories of things. The commentary states:
This is an explanation.
Since this very space has already become manifold,
each individual part is itself designated as "space";
it does not depend on any other time or further categories to be called space.
"Or other categories of things" refers to various designations such as "the self" (*ātman*) and so forth.
If each of these were individually distinguished and named "space" or "the self," [they would likewise be non-existent].
This would contradict your own tenet that space (*ākāśa*) and the self (*ātman*) are both all-pervasive and eternal.
Alternatively, it may be explained thus:
these many portions of space are merely designated by names according to their respective substrata.
It does not depend on other times to establish its name.
For example, when it is associated with the time of spring, the name is established solely based on the meaning of unobstructedness during that springtime;
it does not further depend on other times, such as autumn or winter, to separately establish its name.
The same applies to other instances of the Vaipulya [sūtras].
Since space here is established with distinct names according to its respective bases,
we know that space is composed of immeasurable parts.
Regarding "or other categories of things":
it is not only the sense of being unobstructed with respect to time, space, and objects that is designated as "space" (*ākāśa*);
rather, the sense of absolute non-existence with respect to time, space, and objects is also designated as "the hair of a tortoise" or "the horns of a rabbit."
However, since the hare and its horns,
as well as the tortoise and its hair, are both members of the same category of things, they are referred to as "categories of things" (*vastujāti*).
Yet, the horns do not exist upon the hare.
Because hair does not exist on a tortoise,
the hare’s horn and the tortoise’s hair are used to signify the meaning of non-existence.
Thus, both "empty space" and "the hare’s horn" are names established based on their conventional meanings.
One must not rely on names and cling to them as having substantial reality.
Question:
Since space is admitted to be conventionally existent, one must not deprecate it by saying it does not exist.
The horns of a rabbit fundamentally signify non-existence;
how can they be cited as an analogy? Answer:
In terms of their conceptual definitions, existence and non-existence differ;
they are distinct from space and a rabbit’s horns.
Yet when one exhaustively investigates their essential nature, both are equally non-existent.
Therefore, it may be cited as an illustration.
The treatise states:
"Consequently, the meaning of 'reaching cause' (*prāpti-hetu*) as you conceive it is not established. Commentary:
This is the fault of the argument.
Therefore, your proposed proof that space is eternal on the grounds of its omnipresence is unestablished.
Because this space is established as having immeasurable parts rather than being all-pervasive;
that is, it is the fallacy of "non-establishment for one of the two parties" (anyatarāsiddha).
As the treatise says:
If it is argued that [the arguments regarding] emptiness and so forth apply here as well, this is also not the case. The commentary states:
The following section refutes the attempted defense.
First, the defense is restated and then rejected in its entirety.
The subsequent refutation by means of reasoning is a general negation of this attempted defense.
If you offer a defense, saying:
The essence of space and so forth pervades the entire dharma-realm;
however, due to the discriminating mind, space is conventionally described as having spatial divisions according to its various differentiated parts.
However, since the essence of space is actually devoid of spatial divisions,
it is not the case that the reason— its being all-pervasive— is unestablished;
this [objection] is incorrect.
The treatise says:
"In reality, there are no spatial parts, because it does not escape the faults previously stated. The commentary states:
From here below, he refutes [the opponent's position] by means of reasoning.
There are four [refutations]:
first, the refutation by the same fault as before; second, the refutation by demonstrating a contradiction in the reason;
third, the refutation by establishing a separate inference (*anumāna*); and fourth, [the refutation by] citing scripture.
The refutation based on the non-establishment of the reason for the four positions is the same as the refutation of the aforementioned fault.
Since space and so forth are neither real nor possess spatial parts, [the reason is unestablished].
If [the atom] pervades all parts, it would become infinitely divisible according to those pervaded parts; you cannot avoid such faults.
The treatise says:
"Vases and the like would also contradict the meaning of 'reaching' (*prāpti*). The commentary states:
This demonstrates a refutation based on the contradiction of the reason (*hetu*).

According to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the thesis that vases and the like must actually lack spatial parts (*digbhāga*) is established by means of [the concept of] spatial parts as mere designations (*prajñapti*). Therefore, the reason—like the example of space—is such that since vases and the like actually lack spatial parts, [the reason is contradictory].
Thus, space and the like would possess the reason of "pervasive presence.
Yet, in your thesis that space is eternal, there is ultimately no similar instance (sapakṣa);
you merely take jars and the like as its dissimilar instances (vipakṣa).
This pervasive cause cannot exist in what is identical while existing in what is different;
among the four types of contradiction, this is the contradiction with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the phenomenon itself.
As the treatise says:
Furthermore, it is established by taking space and so forth as the objective domain. The commentary states:
This is a distinct establishment of an inference (*anumāna*) for the purpose of refutation.
The first two phrases constitute the subject (*dharmin*).
The next two lines constitute the thesis (pakṣadharma).
The next two lines establish the reason (hetu).

To clarify the intention:
these names, words, and sounds, such as "space" and so forth, [are merely conventional designations].

The treatise says:

The reason given was that it can be said to possess spatial parts (*digbhāga*).

that emptiness and so forth are not pervasive contradicts the intrinsic characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*) of those phenomena;

However, since the preceding passage has already raised the objection regarding contradictory reasons (*viruddha-hetu*),
the present section merely demonstrates the fault of non-establishment (*asiddha*) with respect to the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*).
Since the nature of space and so forth is neither eternal nor all-pervasive, [the reason is unestablished].
This constitutes a failure of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) to be established as part of the thesis (*pakṣa*).
Furthermore, since these things such as space (*ākāśa*) are not substantially existent,

This constitutes the fallacy of the unestablished basis (*āśrayāsiddha*) for the proof.
The treatise says:
"Furthermore, there may be [a case where one] reaches the knowledge that real time exists. The commentary states:
The following three verses refute the permanence of time.
The first verse refutes the activity of time;
that is, it refutes it by demonstrating that activity evolves in accordance with conditions.
The second verse refutes the functional capacity of time by means of demonstrating that the cause is not separate from its effect.
The third verse refutes the permanence of time.
This is an immediate refutation based on the necessity of the cause undergoing transformation.
Regarding the first refutation within the section on temporal activity,
it concerns initial origination.
Next, the verse is presented,
followed by its explanation.
Within the introduction, the initial section describes the assertions of external opponents.
The subsequent section clarifies the purpose of the verse;
within the description of the adherents' misconceptions,

"This is the establishment of the thesis (*pakṣa*).

The meaning of this passage is as follows:
At that time, the entity truly exists,
for we directly perceive the seeds, soil, water, human effort, and other conditions combining together;
yet, it arises immediately in the springtime.
Since it does not arise in autumn,
we know that its activity consists of unfolding and rolling up according to the seasons;
that is to say, because its activity of unfolding occurs during springtime.
When the conditions for the seed are assembled, it arises and causes the branches and twigs to flourish;
in autumn, there is a function of contraction,
whereby even though the conditions such as the seed are assembled, it does not arise and causes the branches and twigs to wither and decay.
Regarding this stated reason (hetu) which possesses both separation and conjunction:
"separation" refers to the dissimilar instance (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), while "conjunction" refers to the similar instance (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
This inference is as follows:

The thesis is that time exists as a real entity because it possesses causal activity; the reason is that whatever possesses causal activity is entirely real, just like color and other such phenomena (the similar instance). Conversely, if something were not real, it would lack causal activity, just like a tortoise’s hair and the like (the dissimilar instance).

The treatise says: "By means of this very fact, how could it possibly be permanent? The commentary states: The term *śāstra* (treatise) refers to the *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya*. The phrase "by means of this very fact" (*anenaiva vastunā*) refers to the aforementioned proof that conditioned phenomena are impermanent. The phrase "how could it possibly be permanent" (*kutaḥ śāśvato bhavet*) indicates that since all conditioned things are established as impermanent, there is no possibility whatsoever for anything to be permanent. This is because permanence and the nature of conditioned arising are mutually exclusive. If one were to claim that something is permanent despite its being subject to causes and conditions, such a position would contradict the very definition of conditioned phenomena and would render the categories of existence and non-existence incoherent. Thus, the logical conclusion is that nothing produced by causes can be eternal. This establishes the thesis (*pakṣa*) that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent through the application of the reason (*hetu*) and the supporting examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). The reason—that they arise in dependence upon others—is supported by the examples of earth, which changes according to the elements it encounters, and color, which varies according to light and other conditions. Since these are clearly observed to be impermanent, the same must apply to all conditioned entities. Therefore, the argument stands: conditioned phenomena are definitively impermanent. The commentary concludes by reiterating that given this established principle, the notion of permanence is untenable.
This is the destruction of the substantial entity (*dravya*).
One takes this aforementioned instance of the color of earth as a factual example (*dṛṣṭānta*) to serve as the "similar instance" (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) for the subsequent inference (*anumāna*).
